label: text
text: In the course of a description of the scenes on board H.M.S. Repulse as the vessel crossed the line, Mr. G. Ward Price, the "Daily Mail" special correspondent says:

label: text
text: . Precariously lying across the front like a recumbent green Egyptian mummy was the "lovely daughter," who Neptune announced overnight would be presented to the Prince.

label: text
text: A fanfare of trumpets burst suddenly from the forecastle, and down the deck towards a platform high above a great sailcloth tank, filled to a depth of 4 feet with sea water, came Neptune and Queen Amphitrite. They were in a chariot, the basis of which appeared to be the gun-cauga of a Marines field-piece.

label: text
text: Her immobility was due to the stiffness of her fishy tail. Her golden hair hung below her waist, her white shoulders gleamed in the sun, but fingers as deeply stained by cigarette smoking as any midshipman's seemed to indicate that modern vices have spread even to the ocean bed.

text: Ten "bears" roaring dismally in thick pelts of brown tow drow their scaly majesties to the Prince. The proceedings then lapsed into very fishy verse, as perforated by Neptune:—

label: text
text: In the divorce lists published for the Easter Law Sittings, the undefended petitions outnumber the defended cases by 4 to 1.

label: text
text: Among the undefended cases is that of the Marquis of Queensberry, who is citing Sir James Dunn as co-respondent. Lady Dunn is also seeking a divorce.

label: text
text: The Marquis of Queensberry, who is 29, succeeded to the title in 1920 and married in 1917 Irene Richards, a Gaiety actress and daughter of a millowner. There is one daughter aged seven. Sir James Dunn is a Canadian barrister aged 50. His home is in New Brunswick.

label: text
text: Another undefended suit is that of Lady Kitty Vincent, who is asking for a divorce from her husband, Brigadier-General Sir Berkeley Vincent. Before her marriage in 1906 she was Lady Kitty Ogilvy, eldest daughter of the late Earl of Airlie.

label: text
text: The defended suits include that of Viscount Gort, V.C., who is seeking a divorce from Viscountess Gort. Viscount Gort is a lieutenant-colonel in the Grenadier Guards. He won the V.C. in 1918 in the attack of the Guards Division across the Canal du Nord. He also holds the D.S.O. with two bars and the M.C. He was wounded nine times.

label: text
text:
During the war Lady Gort sold hats in a business she started in Grosvenor Street. The profits were given to the Red Cross.

label: paragraph_title
text: DEAD", GIRL

label: paragraph_title
text: "I HOPE HE WILL BE PUNISHED:"

label: text
text: Allegations against a prominent Lincolnshire farmer and landowner were made in a letter addressed to the coroner by Kate Helena Leesing, 20, a domestic servant who poisoned herself at North Thoresby.

label: text
text:
At the inquest the coroner, Mr. Sharpley, of Louth, read the following letter:—
I have not done this terrible thing because I wanted to die, but a statement I have made to a solicitor can be shown to you.
When I told Mr. Sands my suspicions he told me to be sure to blame someone else. Who does he think I can blame? I shall not blame an innocent man for what he has done, and I only hope he will be very severely punished for causing this to happen. He is the father of my child, no matter what he says.
Mr. Sands, I hope, will never know what it is to have a peaceful mind for the rest of his life. (Signed) Kate Leesing.

label: text
text: Mr. Iveson, a solicitor of Hull, said that Mrs. Sands, wife of Mr. Thomas Sands, of Gainsby, had instructed his firm to institute divorce proceedings on her behalf, and Miss Leesing was cited as co-respondent.

label: text
text: William Leesing, father of the girl, said he knew his daughter was worried because Mr. Sands, she said, had asked her to blame somebody else. The girl had interviewed solicitors with regard to the pending divorce suit.

label: text
text:
Harriet Leesing, the mother, said that since she became aware of her daughter's condition she had learned that the girl had been in the company of Mr. Sands at Grimsby and other places.
Some time ago the girl was charged with obtaining clothing by false pretences. Her story then was that Mr. Sands authorised her to get the goods in his name and though this was denied heard the case discharged her.
A doctor said the girl had taken salts of lemon, and Mr. Iveson suggested that Mr. Sands should be called.

label: text
text:
The Coroner: I am not going to shield Sands. He must know about the girl's death, and if he wanted to come here to make a statement he could have done so. If he is morally to blame it must rest on his conscience. There is nothing to show he has been in her company lately.
A verdict of Suicide while Temporarily Insane was returned.
